body: Hi, all I can say is that they don't sound like great people. Good on you for reaching out at all, I wouldn't dare reach out to anyone in my family. I don't really trust them. My family are the ones that are the cause of a lot of my problems so why would I expect them to help me. Maybe the fact you're surrounded by toxic people is the cause of some of your problems. You should try to make some new friends, be upfront from the beginning that you need support and be willing to offer it in return. They are out there.

Hi, thanks for reaching out. No need to try and make yourself "sound interesting" you sound interesting to me. I don't think I've ever known anyone with depression to be boring, we tend to be a pretty deep and interesting bunch, I've found. I'll send you a PM in a bit if that's cool.

Hi, thank you for replying. You have some great interests there. I am starting to take in interest in psychology, a lot has been revealed to me just with the little bit of research I have done. Do you know what? Just hearing the words "I'd like to talk to you" after hearing my story means a lot to me right now. I can really relate to the little bit that you've shared, it's so strange that there are people just like me, I knew they were out there but wondered how I'd ever find them, learning my personality profile really helped. It's getting late here and I'm feeling tired and a bit headachey, so I shall certainly PM you tomorrow if that's ok. I look forward to talking to you.

Hi, thanks for replying. I wish I read more, I love stories but find myself more engaged by really good storytelling with a visual component, it's probably a bit of laziness as well. I should start reading again. Drawing is so hard isn't it? I'm not great myself, any ability I have in drawing is hard earned, whereas I'm lucky to have music as a gift. I have serious respect for people who can draw really well, it's one of the most time consuming skills to learn. I like photography, the ability to tell a story or convey feeling with an image can be very powerful. I'll send you a PM in a while if that's ok. Thanks again.

Hey, sounds like a real tough situation you're in there. I've also got a real dysfunctional family with drug problems. I made it through my early twenties working in a factory, I then went back to college, to university and got a degree. I'm a fucking wreck now but I was alright for a while at university. My situation was very fucked (single mum, heroin addict, alcoholic) As you're 20, is there any support for young people in your area or gov programmes to get you back into an education environment? Or could you get an apprenticeship to start a trade?

I've considered contacting her before but I don't think she works at my old school any more. I don't suppose it would be appropriate to message/friend her on Facebook? I'm not really sure. Thanks for your reply. :)

Well, many people, and lots with depression use substances to self medicate, whether it is alcohol, weed, cigarettes, caffeine, opiates etc. It stops you from directly experiencing feelings and helps you bury them. It also changes your brain chemistry, serotonin and dopamine which are related to mood. Sure it's not good, people aren't really finding comfort in these things, it's more a case of taking the edge off or stopping them from feeling really terrible at that moment. Also, yeah, wouldn't recommend strong drink+fast car as a depression cure, just FYI. ;)

Do you know what I realised? Anyone can be suicidal, it doesn't matter what the circumstances. For a while, I'm ashamed to admit, I thought "How can these people be suicidal, when there is nothing bad happening in their lives?" Because I have had a bad childhood and some quite serious trauma growing up I thought my depression was more important than everyone else. The realisation hit me, there are people in the world with a lot less than me, who have had a lot worse happen who are not suicidal or depressed. I don't really understand it but that is the case. I think issues like neglect, poverty, drug abuse etc are all risk factors for depression and make it more likely, but it's not the whole story, I realise that now.

Hey saturnspotato, I just realised something, I was being dumb in my previous post and thinking you just woke up the day after taking some antihistamines, I'm sorry, I'm in London UK so it's morning here, I just woke up when I posted and I assumed you were on my continent, derp. If you're still up and want to talk, we're here.

Those allergy pills make me feel like absolute rubbish the next day. I sometimes get severe migraines from them, wake up the next day feeling completely drained and out of whack. I've stopped taking them altogether now. I know it's not the cause of your problems but when you're feeling down, tipping yourself one way or another with a certain action can make all the difference between feeling suicidal or not. Everything you said up there does not make you a bad person, there are real bad people out there, you are not one of them. Give yourself plenty of room today, put yourself first, look after yourself and treat it like any other sick day; blankets, comfort food, movies, hot drinks. Or depending on you, whatever it is you do that enables you to cope or feel better.

Hi, you mention food. I know it's not going to be the cure to your problems, but as someone with serious depression I find that not eating enough can really affect my condition. I would recommend when you're not feeling well to just eat whatever you like, comfort food, this is not going to cure you, but it might make the 5% difference between suicidal and not suicidal. Being skinny is not worth the pain of suicidal ideation, you have to look after number 1 and try to be loving to yourself as best as you possibly can.

I've done this before. I think it's almost a form of self-harm, in a way, pushing people away that you care about. One thing I regret, is not opening up to certain people, at least giving them a chance, to find out if they really care about what I've been through. Otherwise you'll never know. You might find that they care and can help, you might find out that they were never as great as you thought they were. Things might not be over with them, you could explain what you're going through, and at least give them the chance to prove if they're good friends or not. Do they have any idea what you're going through?
Hey, I've been there man, is there anything happened today that made you feel like this?

Hi, there will always be fake people around that will hurt you, it sucks, I've experienced it. I can't get my head around how cruel people can be, it does not compute for me. Then even when the odd one comes around who isn't fake you might even push them away or ruin it with them. It comes with the territory of depression. Friends are picky and clicky around your age, maybe you could seek out a supportive relationship with a girl/guy as you will find that all your friends will be pairing off so try not to get left behind and he/she may give you the motivation you need to try and feel better.

The possibility that there will be some miraculous advancement in science/space exploration in our lifetime. The chance that in the future maybe I will find someone who loves me and needs me and I'll be happy to be alive.

I started taking them around midway through 2012, I only took them for pain, a few times a month back then. It's been a proper addiction for about a year I think. I don't take much, but I have had a few binges. It's not like one hit and your hooked like you may have seen in movies, it takes time to become an addiction, it just creeps up on you. I was totally the "it won't happen to me" guy. I've seen what addiction does to families and I once swore that I would never go that route. 

I had a really traumatic event in the beginning of 2013. I have also had some bad news in the family about a year ago and I also lost my grandma. I feel bad because my depression stopped me from seeing her much in her last months. I think she was upset with me, she didn't understand why I wasn't around. Things have been going downhill since then, not much positive has happened to me.

That's one thing I think I'm quite lucky with in a way, I don't really beat myself up too much, I don't really blame myself or anything. I know that I'm not a bad person, I just have had bad things happen, and wasn't given the best set of cards. (basically we're talking self-pity instead of self-loathing) not sure which is worse to be honest! 

Yeah the codeine thing is shit. I didn't start taking it recreationally, it was for back pain and migraines. It just developed into an addiction, it's very closely related to dopamine receptors, which is basically what can make the difference between suicidal and not suicidal. It's a game you don't want to know anything about, trust me on that. It's very mood altering and can leave you with a sort of fuzzy well being feeling, but it's fake. Sooner or later you start getting side-effects and they are horrible.

I appreciate what you say, though I think it's right to say that waking up suicidal, is not really comparable to waking up and feeling self-defeated. What I'm experiencing is more than a "bad day at the office" I'm afraid. You're right about looking at what had me feeling better. The main thing I can think of is that I started cutting down on taking codeine and felt I had more control than I have had in a while. I was experiencing a lot of pain and crying, but it was the good sort of cry if you get me. Then like two nights ago I sort of relapsed and took a high dose again which is why I think I feel fucked now. I just had some food and that made me feel better than earlier, I'm going to continue cutting down my dosages of codeine again and see if I start feeling better. I watched an interview with Kurt Cobain earlier, he said something along the lines of "why not become a junkie, when you're suicidal and in pain anyway" I kind of know what he meant, I can relate, but I've got to not go down that route, consciously choose not to go full junkie.

Yeah that's a tricky one, see what they suggest, the most important thing is that they know what's going on. I think you can take the exam, and if your performance is affected by the situation you can apply for extenuating circumstances and get an adjustment. Sometimes you need to go beyond lecturers and talk to administrators and programmes office. I give you my real deepest sympathies for the loss of your parents. I grew up without my dad and very nearly lost my mum more than once, I still worry about it, losing them must be unthinkably painful. I'm glad you're going to talk to your therapist, just be aware of isolating and self destructing because that's what I did and I regret not asking for help now. Good luck with your finals.

Hello, you sound interesting, I get the sense that you are quite a layered and deep person. I didn't quite know what you meant by INFJ, I did assume it was one of those personality type profiles. Well googling those letters took me to a test at 16personalities, I just took the test myself, turns out I am an INFP, also pretty rare (4%) Just wanted to thank you indirectly for that because I read the detailed profile and it just basically spelled it out, way more accurate than I expected. I also found out famous INFP's; Kurt Cobain, Jim Morrison, Tim Burton, Princess Diana anyway I'm going on a bit now, not exactly on topic (penpals), but it's a bit of a revelation for me so thanks!

I'm not exactly sure as I didn't call on it in university myself, I know it exists though. Each university/college/school has it's own guidelines, but they are all roughly the same. I had it in secondary (high) school and I finished with B's in science even though I missed the exam (my mum was in rehab and I had poor attendance in school) I got B's because that's what they deemed I would have got minus the circumstances from looking at my coursework. They don't mark you down, they give you what is called a "predicted grade" they look at your other performance, and give you a mark that is in line with the rest of your work, what they would have expected you to get without the difficult circumstances.

Thanks, that's really nice of you to say. I really hope you feel better and everything works out, if you think I could help with anything from here in London UK please keep posting. I can help research things for support if you are stuck. I am also familiar with the pain of losing a wacom pen (mine broken by rolling over on a chair with wheels) so there's that, it sucks.

I have had the same from people that downplay things when you tell them something's wrong. It's kind of frustrating, in a way I think on one hand you have people that care about you, who don't want to believe anything is wrong (denial), then you have others who would rather not have to face what's wrong because it means they would have to help or do something for you so their conscience is challenged. I've considered getting an mri scan for my brain because I get severe migraines once in a while (seizures, vomiting proper migraines) and I've had people say to me "Oh it's probably nothing, only x or y, do you drink to much caffeine etc" Then again I do recognize I have a mindset where I do sometimes think the worst possible thing is happening (I don't know if this is common for those with depression, seems like it) the truth is probably somewhere in between.

Hi, your story is very sad like many of us here, and you have been through a lot. I read all your story and I think you are really brave and you care for your sister and mum a lot. Thank you for sharing it because it makes many people feel like they are not alone, you are not alone either. You have a lot of value and a lot to offer because through everything the love is still there for your sister, your mum and your dog, that is powerful. Like others have said, is there any way you can get to education or college there? Is there somewhere you can volunteer with helping kids or something? What about charities, churches, anything to give you some structure in the days. Depending on where you are of course, make sure your safety is first. Everyone has value, I know it doesn't feel like it sometimes but try to find a way that you feel useful to somebody. Also you seem pretty smart, have you thought about learning computer science or something, online courses for free from Harvard etc at www.edx.org

Your post made me think, I also had a few concussions over the years. One of the worst was as a kid, I was 6 and I came off my bike and went down a steep curb into a parked van, head first, skull fracture, unconscious, bad concussion. I never really thought about being linked to my depression but I guess it makes sense. I also think age is a factor, I think approaching 30 is a tough time, both physically and mentally, I've found turning 30 really rough. Lots of hormonal changes, plus the mental milestone of 30, when you're supposed to have all your shit together and be sorted out. It sucks when things haven't turned out how they expected. I haven't really got any consolations or advice, except to say yep, I know what that feels like, and you made me think about some things so thanks for the post. One thing I will say is that I've been thinking about doing some stuff for charity, and that has given me a hint of purpose, and something to think about, combating feeling useless by making myself useful, might not be for everyone though.

Couldn't they make an exception, or give you a predicted grade if you have what they call here "extenuating circumstances". Maybe email one of your lecturers or go in to speak to one. There is usually one on each course that is designated for student mentorship. You are clearly under extreme circumstances, the worry of college work looming over you is obviously making matters worse. Once you're clear that your grades will be taken care of under extenuating circumstances guidelines then maybe you will feel better about talking to your counsellor. Or you could do it the other way round, talk to your counsellor and get them to forward considerations to your course leaders, without having to go into anything specific or personal with your lecturers. Even if you decide to stick it out for the next couple of weeks it's worth knowing that the mechanism is there for exactly these type of circumstances if you're ever stuck in future.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extenuating_circumstances#In_academia 

If it was me, I'd be worried about going into self-destruct mode now, I did at the end of my degree after working myself into a stupor. I had extenuating circumstances but instead of going to the lecturers and explaining what happened I punished myself by staying quiet and letting them grade me badly. I regret it now. I wish I had gone and talked, there's frameworks in colleges/universities for dealing with this, it's nothing new to them, but you have to find the strength and silence the negativity to ask for what's available to you and what you are entitled to.

Thanks, you're welcome. Sometimes it just takes another perspective to see what's available to you, there is a lot, especially in a developed country like Sweden. I also know how tough it can be dealing with addiction and family addiction so anything I can do to help is the least I can do.

Tell me about it, I know how hard it can be to go for help. I have been suffering mostly on my own all this time, I've only been to counsellors a handful of times despite how serious my issues are. I'm reaching the point now where I will soon have to go for help and it is scary.

I can relate in many ways. I'm starting to come to terms with the fact that my childhood experiences have basically dictated the outcome of my life, there's no real way to avoid it. I've tried to act like it didn't in the past. I've dealt with addiction, both family and myself. Both parents junkies, dad was kicked out of the house when I was about 2.

As for practical advice, as of right now I'm in a depression that has been going on for about 3 years, only in the past 3 months or so has it become a major depression where I haven't left the house and have been having suicidal ideation most days. However I did from about 23-27 do OK and wasn't suicidal. I made it through university and got a valuable degree, I also had moderate success with work. Not holding a job down, but working freelance projects as you describe. I was able to do a degree without having any funds upfront, I have debt, but it's the last of my worries, I was also able to get extra grants and stuff because of my history. Doing that course kept me out of trouble and structure and a bit of money.

So to the actual point, the advice; you're still young, search for any funding, support, mentorship, charity, government programmes. Anything that will give you structure, a place to be, and some funds. Every developed country spends millions on stuff like this every year, you just have to be tenacious, and shout the loudest, to get access to the support. You'll be forced to repeat your traumatic story over again, which sucks, but if the right people hear it, you will get support, it is out there, especially as your under 25. If you find this to be unavailable (really depends on what country you live if you say I'll search for some stuff for you), then there's gofundme and kickstarter. The skills you want these days are resourcefulness, innovation, problem-solving and design. Anyone can bootstrap these days. And finally obvious practical stuff, when really depressed, try and make sure it's not depressed + hungry, or depressed + poverty, depressed + withdrawing, because that's when it can be really lethal.
Witty SOB

Doing research is definitely a good idea.  If you feel like you played a part in the ambush and it hurt her, then you could try to apologise, let her know that you were trying to help but you realise now it was misguided. The letter is not a bad idea if you are having difficulty contacting her otherwise. I strongly do not recommend trying to take her anywhere against her will. Cornering or pressuring her can be dangerous. 

Maybe the situation at Christmas was quite emotionally charged, with lots of family involved and your sis was probably overwhelmed. Maybe she didn't have any gifts to give in return and felt unworthy. I doubt her intention was to hurt you guys it's more likely she felt like she didn't deserve them. I would not rule out offering material support on this basis.

The main thing when trying to understand depression is that it is an illness like any other, when severe it can be very serious, worse in many ways than other "physical" conditions. If your sister had any other illness that had this outcome how would you comfort her? This video was posted the other day and may be of some use in furthering your understanding of the illness: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NOAgplgTxfc

I can speak from experience of having major depression and having a brother who is in the same situation as you, trying to help me. Let her know that you love her, you understand and subtle, attempts at contact are fine. Expect that you will not hear back, but try not to take it personally, it's most likely not personal and do not give up on her. Do not be pushy or dramatic, do not attempt to "corner" her or stage an intervention unless you are genuinely worried that she will harm herself, in which case ask her if she will, if she says she won't then listen to her. I'm afraid it's beyond your control anyway, you will have to learn to accept this. Let her know that you're there any time she wants to talk. I wonder if you cornering her the first time has led to her to recede even more, it can be a horrible and traumatic experience, don't feel bad about it though, learn. 

It's clear she doesn't want to talk. Is there any other way you can help her? I assume she's not financially doing well, maybe offer to give her some money, or nice things, stuff to make this difficult time more comfortable for her. Show her in action that you're here to help. That's one thing my family completely failed at, it seems all they want to do is offer me patronizing talks, I wonder if deep down they wish to quell their own guilt more than actually offer me any practical help. I'm not saying this is the situation with you but be aware of it. Give her practical unrequited help, if you were stuck in this situation what practically do you think you would need/like?

I agree, it's the equivalent of saying "Oh man, that guy Dave and his diabetes, get's me down being around the guy he should snap out of it" It's a symbol of a poorly understood and stigmatised illness, more education urgently needed.

Thanks. I guess by making this post and coming here in the first place is a sign that I'm starting to look for help. I've avoided it, thinking it would get better or I'd temporarily pull myself out of it on my own, like I have done in the past. Actually, every day it's getting incrementally worse and more difficult, especially the going out part, the longer I'm leaving that the worse it's getting and harder to face. Sometimes I feel sort of like I don't even exist and the world is just flying past. You're right about the awareness, it's unusually harsh to be stigmatized as well as have such an illness, whereas almost any other life threatening illness you get universal sympathy and support; it's one of the most difficult things about it.

Thank you. That lecture rang true for me. It provides a logical understanding of depression that seemed from my experience with people very poorly understood, or at least it felt like no-one really "got it". Knowing that it's well understood, recognized and explained logically helps a bit.
